Getting started with bicountbrms

Source: vignettes/bicountbrms.Rmd
bicountbrms.Rmd
library(brms)
library(bicountbrms)
library(posterior)
library(dplyr)

bicountbrms models pairs of counts of the same events recorded by two sources, such as two observers or two survey methods. The quantities usually of interest are the amount recorded by the two sources, the extent to which their records agree, and the direction and size of any imbalance between them. This vignette simulates paired counts with known values of these quantities, fits a model that estimates them, and checks the estimates against the true values.

The package has two brms custom families (Bürkner 2017), binegbin, with negative-binomial components, and bipois, with Poisson components, so models are fitted, used for prediction, and compared with the usual brms functions. Each family has two constructors: binegbin() and bipois() for data in which both counts were recorded on every row, and binegbin_partialobs() and bipois_partialobs() for partially paired data, in which source 1 has missing values. This vignette uses binegbin().

The generative model

Each observed count is the sum of a latent count recorded by both sources and a latent count recorded by that source alone, a construction known as ‘trivariate reduction’. Holgate (1964) and Karlis and Ntzoufras (2003) use this construction with Poisson components, Kirkpatrick and Neale (2016) and Kirkpatrick (2022) with negative-binomial components. binegbin() takes all three latent counts to be independent and negative binomial:

\begin{aligned} N_s &\sim \mathrm{NB2}(\mu,\ \phi_s) \\ N_1 &\sim \mathrm{NB2}(\lambda_1,\ \phi_{x1}) \qquad N_2 \sim \mathrm{NB2}(\lambda_2,\ \phi_{x2}) \\[4pt] y_1 &= N_s + N_1 \qquad y_2 = N_s + N_2 \end{aligned}

N_s, the shared component, is the latent count recorded by both sources. N_1 and N_2, the source-exclusive components, are the latent counts recorded by one source only. The shared component induces the positive correlation between y_1 and y_2. N_s is never observed, and the likelihood sums over its possible values k = 0, \dots, \min(y_1, y_2).

NB2(m, phi) is neg_binomial_2 in Stan and dnbinom(size = phi, mu = m) in R: mean m, variance m + m^2/phi. Larger phi means less overdispersion.

In the native parameterisation, binegbin() has six distributional parameters (dpars), all with a log link:

Parameter Meaning Name in brms
\mu rate of the shared component mu
\lambda_1, \lambda_2 rates of the two source-exclusive components lambdaone, lambdatwo
\phi_s NB2 dispersion of the shared component shapes
\phi_{x1}, \phi_{x2} NB2 dispersions of the two exclusive components shapexone, shapextwo

The dpar mu is the rate of the shared component rather than the mean of either count, so that E[y_1] = \mu + \lambda_1. brms requires every custom family to have a dpar named mu.

The congruence–bias parameterisation

bicountbrms provides an interpretable reparameterisation of the model, the congruence–bias parameterisation, in which the coordinates directly represent the quantities usually of interest in a comparison of two sources: the midpoint M, the average amount recorded by the two sources; the congruence f, the extent to which their records agree; and the source bias \beta, the direction and size of any imbalance between them. The three dispersions are replaced by overdispersions \kappa, for which \kappa = 0 is a Poisson component. The helper function bf_mfd() returns the brms formula for this model, and takes one argument for each coordinate in the table below.

Coordinate Meaning Definition Name in brms
M midpoint of the expected counts of the two sources M = \mu + (\lambda_1 + \lambda_2)/2 logM, for \log M
f congruence, the proportion of M recorded by both sources f = \mu / M logitf, for \operatorname{logit} f
\beta source bias, zero when the two exclusive rates are equal \beta = (\lambda_1 - \lambda_2)/(\lambda_1 + \lambda_2) delta, for \operatorname{artanh}\beta
\kappa_s, \kappa_{x1}, \kappa_{x2} overdispersions \kappa = 1/\sqrt{\phi} kappas, kappaxone, kappaxtwo

The interactive widget in the article The congruence–bias parameterisation simulates pairs of counts from one model and shows both parameterisations side by side: moving a slider for one parameterisation moves the sliders for the other, and the plot shows the expected decomposition of each count and the simulated pairs.

We generally recommend the congruence–bias parameterisation. The native parameterisation might be useful when a predictor is expected to affect one latent component only, such as a change in the equipment used by one source (see Models with predictors).

A worked example

Simulate data from known parameters

The true values are set as midpoint, congruence, source bias, and overdispersions. mfd_to_dpars() converts them to the six native dpars, and rbicount() draws the three latent counts and returns them with the two observed counts.

set.seed(20260724)

truth <- list(
  M         = 10,
  f         = 0.75,
  beta      = 0.2,
  kappas    = 0.5,
  kappaxone = 0.4,
  kappaxtwo = 0.7
)

dpars <- mfd_to_dpars(
  M         = truth$M,
  f         = truth$f,
  delta     = atanh(truth$beta),
  kappas    = truth$kappas,
  kappaxone = truth$kappaxone,
  kappaxtwo = truth$kappaxtwo
)

dat <- do.call(rbicount, c(list(n = 400), dpars))

head(dat)
#>   y1 y2 Ns N1 N2
#> 1 17 12 11  6  1
#> 2 10 10  7  3  3
#> 3  5  4  2  3  2
#> 4 13 13 10  3  3
#> 5  7 10  5  2  5
#> 6 11 11  9  2  2
cor(dat$y1, dat$y2)
#> [1] 0.8470486

The correlation is positive and substantial because both counts include the same Ns.

A model with intercepts only

A model in the congruence–bias parameterisation is fitted by specifying its formula with the helper function bf_mfd(). The first argument of bf_mfd() is the response, y1 | vint(y2): a brms custom family has one response, so y1 is the response and y2 is passed to the family as supplementary integer data through vint(). Each further argument is the formula of one parameter in the table above, here ~ 1 for all six, so that each coordinate is the same on every row. The argument stanvars = binegbin_stanvars() adds the Stan function binegbin_lpmf to the functions block of the model; without it, the model does not compile.

fit <- brm(
  bf_mfd(
    y1 | vint(y2),
    logM      ~ 1,
    logitf    ~ 1,
    delta     ~ 1,
    kappas    ~ 1,
    kappaxone ~ 1,
    kappaxtwo ~ 1
  ),
  family   = binegbin(),
  stanvars = binegbin_stanvars(),
  data     = dat,
  prior    = c(
    prior(normal(2, 1),   class = "b", nlpar = "logM"),
    prior(normal(0, 1.5), class = "b", nlpar = "logitf"),
    prior(normal(0, 0.5), class = "b", nlpar = "delta"),
    prior(normal(0, 1),   class = "b", nlpar = "kappas",    lb = 0),
    prior(normal(0, 1),   class = "b", nlpar = "kappaxone", lb = 0),
    prior(normal(0, 1),   class = "b", nlpar = "kappaxtwo", lb = 0)
  ),
  chains  = 2,
  iter    = 1500,
  refresh = 0,
  backend = "cmdstanr",  # or "rstan"
  seed    = 1
)

Unless a prior is specified, brms gives each non-linear parameter a flat, improper prior, so we recommend setting a prior on every coordinate. Each prior has class = "b" and the name of its parameter. The prior normal(2, 1) on logM places 95% of its mass between 1 and 52 on the scale of M, which suits these simulated counts. For other data, we suggest centring it on the log of a plausible midpoint rather than widening its SD, because a wider normal prior on the log scale places more mass on implausibly small and large values (Smith et al. 2020, supplement 3, Fig. S3-1). With an intercept alone in the formula for logitf, the prior normal(0, 1.5) gives a density for f within 10% of uniform between 0.1 and 0.9 (McElreath 2020). The source bias and the overdispersions each have a finite null, \delta = 0 for no source bias and \kappa = 0 for a Poisson component, so their priors have their mode at zero and shrink the estimates towards the simpler model unless the data support otherwise (Simpson et al. 2017). In the native parameterisation, a Poisson component is the limit \phi \to \infty, which no prior on \phi can have as its mode. The bound lb = 0 makes each prior on an overdispersion half-normal.

Convergence 

summary(fit)
#>  Family: binegbin 
#>   Links: mu = log; lambdaone = log; lambdatwo = log; shapes = log; shapexone = log; shapextwo = log 
#> Formula: y1 | vint(y2) ~ 1 
#>          mu ~ logM + log_inv_logit(logitf)
#>          lambdaone ~ log(2) + logM + log1m_inv_logit(logitf) + log_inv_logit(2 * delta)
#>          lambdatwo ~ log(2) + logM + log1m_inv_logit(logitf) + log_inv_logit(-2 * delta)
#>          shapes ~ -2 * log(kappas)
#>          shapexone ~ -2 * log(kappaxone)
#>          shapextwo ~ -2 * log(kappaxtwo)
#>          logM ~ 1
#>          logitf ~ 1
#>          delta ~ 1
#>          kappas ~ 1
#>          kappaxone ~ 1
#>          kappaxtwo ~ 1
#>    Data: dat (Number of observations: 400) 
#>   Draws: 2 chains, each with iter = 1500; warmup = 750; thin = 1;
#>          total post-warmup draws = 1500
#> 
#> Regression Coefficients:
#>                     Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Rhat Bulk_ESS Tail_ESS
#> logM_Intercept          2.32      0.03     2.27     2.37 1.00      935      726
#> logitf_Intercept        1.01      0.17     0.67     1.31 1.00      368      560
#> delta_Intercept         0.18      0.03     0.12     0.25 1.00      515      776
#> kappas_Intercept        0.53      0.04     0.46     0.63 1.00      457      729
#> kappaxone_Intercept     0.44      0.10     0.23     0.62 1.00      459      628
#> kappaxtwo_Intercept     0.48      0.17     0.10     0.81 1.00      360      217
#> 
#> Draws were sampled using sample(hmc). For each parameter, Bulk_ESS
#> and Tail_ESS are effective sample size measures, and Rhat is the potential
#> scale reduction factor on split chains (at convergence, Rhat = 1).

summary(fit) reports, for each parameter, the potential scale reduction factor \hat{R} and the bulk and tail effective sample sizes, and brms warns after sampling if any transitions diverged. A value of \hat{R} above 1.01 indicates that the chains have not converged to the same distribution, and an effective sample size below about 100 per chain indicates too few effectively independent draws for reliable estimates of the posterior quantiles (Vehtari et al. 2021). The summary gives each parameter on the scale of its formula: \log M, \operatorname{logit} f, \operatorname{artanh}\beta, and \kappa.

Recovery of the generating values

The table gives the posterior median (est) and the 95% credible interval (q2.5 to q97.5) of each parameter on its natural scale, with the true value that generated the counts.

recovery <- as_draws_df(fit) |>
  mutate_variables(
    M         = exp(b_logM_Intercept),
    f         = plogis(b_logitf_Intercept),
    beta      = tanh(b_delta_Intercept),
    kappas    = b_kappas_Intercept,
    kappaxone = b_kappaxone_Intercept,
    kappaxtwo = b_kappaxtwo_Intercept
  ) |>
  subset_draws(variable = names(truth)) |>
  summarise_draws(
    est = median,
    ~ quantile2(.x, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))
  ) |>
  mutate(
    truth   = unlist(truth)[variable],
    covered = truth >= q2.5 & truth <= q97.5
  )

knitr::kable(recovery, digits = 2)
variable est q2.5 q97.5 truth covered
M 10.22 9.71 10.72 10.00 TRUE
f 0.73 0.66 0.79 0.75 TRUE
beta 0.18 0.12 0.25 0.20 TRUE
kappas 0.53 0.46 0.63 0.50 TRUE
kappaxone 0.44 0.23 0.62 0.40 TRUE
kappaxtwo 0.48 0.10 0.81 0.70 TRUE

All six 95% intervals contain the true value. The intervals for kappaxone and kappaxtwo are the widest, because the overdispersion of each exclusive component is identified only by the variance of each count beyond that of the shared component.

Prediction

posterior_predict() and posterior_epred() predict the response y_1 only, as for any brms family: posterior_predict() draws y_1 from its marginal distribution, and posterior_epred() returns E[y_1] = \mu + \lambda_1. y_2 is passed to the model as data through vint(), so neither function returns draws of y_2, and pp_check(), fitted(), and conditional_effects(), which call these two functions, show y_1 alone.

posterior_predict_y1_and_y2() draws both counts, and returns an array with one row per draw, one column per row of the data, and one slice for each count. Within each drawn pair, y_1 and y_2 have the same value of N_s, so the correlation between the drawn counts is the correlation under the model. posterior_epred_y1_and_y2() returns the expectations of both counts, \mu + \lambda_1 and \mu + \lambda_2. The table compares the mean, standard deviation, and maximum of each count, and the correlation between the two counts, with the averages of the same quantities over 200 drawn datasets.

yrep <- posterior_predict_y1_and_y2(fit, ndraws = 200)
dim(yrep)
#> [1] 200 400   2

pair_stats <- function(y1, y2) {
  c(
    mean_y1 = mean(y1),
    mean_y2 = mean(y2),
    sd_y1   = sd(y1),
    sd_y2   = sd(y2),
    max_y1  = max(y1),
    max_y2  = max(y2),
    cor     = cor(y1, y2)
  )
}

stats_observed <- pair_stats(dat$y1, dat$y2)

stats_predicted <- yrep |>
  apply(1, \(draw) pair_stats(draw[, "y1"], draw[, "y2"])) |>
  rowMeans()

data.frame(
  observed  = stats_observed,
  predicted = stats_predicted
) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
observed predicted
mean_y1 10.70 10.70
mean_y2 9.73 9.74
sd_y1 5.44 5.36
sd_y2 5.02 5.18
max_y1 36.00 33.29
max_y2 33.00 31.89
cor 0.85 0.84

Prediction and imputation describes the other prediction functions, including posterior_predict_y1_given_y2(), which draws y_1 conditional on the recorded y_2, and so imputes y_1 on rows where y_1 was not recorded.

Model comparison

log_lik() returns, for each row, the log of the joint probability of (y_1, y_2), so loo() estimates the expected log predictive density (elpd) of the pair (Vehtari et al. 2017), and models of the same pair can be compared by their elpd. To compare negative-binomial with Poisson components, we fit bipois(), which has the same construction as binegbin() but with Poisson components (and therefore no overdispersions), to the same data and compare the two fits with loo_compare(). Without the three overdispersions, bf_mfd() returns the formula for bipois().

fit_pois <- brm(
  bf_mfd(
    y1 | vint(y2),
    logM   ~ 1,
    logitf ~ 1,
    delta  ~ 1
  ),
  family   = bipois(),
  stanvars = bipois_stanvars(),
  data     = dat,
  prior    = c(
    prior(normal(2, 1),   class = "b", nlpar = "logM"),
    prior(normal(0, 1.5), class = "b", nlpar = "logitf"),
    prior(normal(0, 0.5), class = "b", nlpar = "delta")
  ),
  chains  = 2,
  iter    = 1500,
  refresh = 0,
  backend = "cmdstanr",  # or "rstan"
  seed    = 1
)
fit      <- add_criterion(fit, "loo")
fit_pois <- add_criterion(fit_pois, "loo")
loo(fit)
#> 
#> Computed from 1500 by 400 log-likelihood matrix.
#> 
#>          Estimate   SE
#> elpd_loo  -2176.1 22.5
#> p_loo         6.2  0.6
#> looic      4352.1 45.1
#> ------
#> MCSE of elpd_loo is 0.1.
#> MCSE and ESS estimates assume MCMC draws (r_eff in [0.3, 1.2]).
#> 
#> All Pareto k estimates are good (k < 0.69).
#> See help('pareto-k-diagnostic') for details.

comparison <- loo_compare(fit, fit_pois)
comparison
#>     model elpd_diff se_diff p_worse diag_diff diag_elpd
#>       fit       0.0     0.0      NA                    
#>  fit_pois    -169.1    30.2    1.00

loo(fit) prints the elpd estimate of the negative-binomial model and a table of Pareto k estimates. A row with a Pareto k estimate above about 0.7 has an unreliable estimate of its elpd (Vehtari et al. 2024). loo_compare() lists the model with the higher elpd first. elpd_diff is the difference in elpd between each model and the first model, and se_diff is the standard error of that difference. The elpd of the Poisson model is lower by 169 (SE 30), so negative-binomial components describe these counts much better than Poisson components, as expected from counts simulated with overdispersions between 0.4 and 0.7.

Models with predictors

Each coordinate has its own formula. A predictor in the formula for logM multiplies all three rates by the same factor, and a predictor in the formula for logitf or delta changes the congruence or the source bias. The formulas below are for data with a factor source1_type, such as the type of equipment used by source 1, and a grouping factor group with many levels; the simulated data above have neither.

In the model below, the formula for logM alone includes a group-level effect of group, so the groups differ in how much the two sources record but not in the extent to which their records agree. The formula for delta includes source1_type, so source1_type changes the balance of exclusive records between the two sources with M and f held fixed. Each coefficient has a prior with class = "b", as in the model with intercepts only, and the SD of the group-level effect on logM has a prior with class = "sd".

fit_groups <- brm(
  bf_mfd(
    y1 | vint(y2),
    logM      ~ 1 + (1 | group),
    logitf    ~ 1,
    delta     ~ source1_type,
    kappas    ~ 1,
    kappaxone ~ 1,
    kappaxtwo ~ 1
  ),
  family   = binegbin(),
  stanvars = binegbin_stanvars(),
  data     = my_data,
  prior    = c(
    prior(normal(2, 1),   class = "b",  nlpar = "logM"),
    prior(normal(0, 1),   class = "sd", nlpar = "logM"),
    prior(normal(0, 1.5), class = "b",  nlpar = "logitf"),
    prior(normal(0, 0.5), class = "b",  nlpar = "delta"),
    prior(normal(0, 1),   class = "b",  nlpar = "kappas",    lb = 0),
    prior(normal(0, 1),   class = "b",  nlpar = "kappaxone", lb = 0),
    prior(normal(0, 1),   class = "b",  nlpar = "kappaxtwo", lb = 0)
  ),
  backend = "cmdstanr",  # or "rstan"
  seed    = 1
)
summary(fit_groups)

In summary(fit_groups), the row delta_source1_typeB is the difference in \operatorname{artanh}\beta between level B of source1_type and the reference level, and the row sd(logM_Intercept), under ~group, is the SD of the group-level effects on \log M.

Native parameterisation

Where a predictor changes one latent component alone, the native parameterisation describes it more simply. In the formula below, only the formula for lambdaone includes source1_type, so source1_type changes the exclusive rate of source 1 and no other rate, and so changes M, f, and \beta together. In this parameterisation, the three rates can be linked across groups only through a group-level effect with a shared ID in each rate formula, (1 | s | group), under which the three effects of a group are correlated rather than equal (Bürkner 2018).

bf(
  y1 | vint(y2) ~ 1 + (1 | s | group),
  lambdaone     ~ 1 + (1 | s | group) + source1_type,
  lambdatwo     ~ 1 + (1 | s | group),
  shapes        ~ 1,
  shapexone     ~ 1,
  shapextwo     ~ 1
)

Further reading

binegbin_partialobs() and bipois_partialobs() fit partially paired designs, in which y_1 was not recorded on some rows, with the response y1 | vint(y2, y1_obs). A partially paired design is fitted in the article Partially paired designs, and Prediction and imputation describes the imputation of the unrecorded values of y_1.

The package skellambrms (Smith 2026) models the difference d = y_1 - y_2 directly. The shared component cancels from d, so a model of d cannot estimate the midpoint or the congruence.
